title: Fair Share
summary: Stop one runaway client from starving everyone else: per-key limits, window and token-bucket algorithms, shared counters and polite 429s.

goals.text: Explain why shared capacity needs per-client limits
Compare fixed windows, sliding windows and token buckets
Enforce one limit across many gateways

steps.title: Anyone may ask anything
body: Skyglass sells weather forecasts through an API. Farms, airlines and app developers each hold an API key and call GET /forecast. Traffic is healthy and the servers are half busy.
Nothing stops a single key from sending as much as it likes. Until now, nobody did.

card.title: Skyglass today
lines: 2,000 customers, each with an API key
# no limits: every key may send anything

steps.title: One bug, everyone's outage
body: Customer #4471 deploys a script with a retry loop and no delay. It hammers the API with 9,000 requests a second — seven times everyone else combined.
The servers don't know whose requests matter. Queues fill, latency soars and requests from all 2,000 customers start failing. This is the noisy neighbour problem.

steps.title: Everyone gets a budget
body: A rate limiter in the gateway counts requests per API key. Up to 20 per second pass; beyond that the gateway answers 429 Too Many Requests immediately, without touching the Forecast API.
The script still misbehaves, but it can only spend its own budget. Everyone else is served normally again.

callout.text: Rejecting is cheap — microseconds in the gateway — so a limiter keeps working even under a flood.

card.title: The polite “no”
lines: # cheap: rejected before any real work

steps.title: Counting per minute
body: The simplest algorithm is a fixed window: keep one counter per key per clock minute and reject once it passes 1,200. It needs one number per key and resets itself.
Its flaw is at the edges. A client can send 1,200 requests at 12:00:59 and 1,200 more at 12:01:00 — twice the intended rate in two seconds.

card.title: Fixed window: count per minute
lines: ! 2,400 requests in 2 seconds — double the limit

steps.title: Smoothing the edges
body: A sliding window judges the last 60 seconds rather than the current clock minute. Storing every timestamp is exact but heavy; the common shortcut weights the previous window's count by how much of it still overlaps.
Two counters per key, no boundary spike, and an error small enough to ignore.

card.title: Sliding window estimate
lines: # 2 counters per key, smooth at edges

steps.title: Allowance with savings
body: A token bucket gives each key a bucket that refills at the allowed rate (20 tokens/s) up to a maximum (40). Each request spends a token; an empty bucket means 429.
Two knobs say two different things: the refill rate caps the long-run average, the bucket size allows short bursts — like an app that fires 30 calls when it opens.

steps.title: Each gateway counts alone
body: Skyglass grows to three gateways behind a load balancer. Each one keeps its counters in its own memory, and the load balancer spreads key #4471 over all three.
Each gateway sees 20 req/s and is happy — so the key actually gets 60. Every gateway you add quietly raises everyone's limit.

card.title: Local counters
lines: each gateway counts on its own
the LB spreads the key over all 3
# add gateways → the limit drifts up

steps.title: One counter for the fleet
body: Move the counters into a shared, fast store like Redis. Each gateway runs an atomic INCR on the key's counter (or a small script for a token bucket) and gets the fleet-wide count in under a millisecond.
Decide what happens if the store is unreachable: fail open (allow traffic, risk overload) is usual for public APIs; fail closed suits limits that guard money or security, like login attempts.

card.title: One count for the whole fleet
lines: # token bucket? one small Lua script
! Redis down → fail open, alert loudly

steps.title: Tell clients how to behave
body: A good limiter explains itself: Retry-After says when to come back and rate-limit headers show the remaining budget. Well-behaved clients back off with jitter, and #4471's fixed script now waits instead of hammering.

Limits are also product choices: bigger plans get bigger budgets, sensitive endpoints like login get tight per-IP limits, and when the backend itself is struggling, load shedding drops low-priority work regardless of who sent it.

card.title: Limits are product decisions
lines: per tenant: cap total, not just per key
# shed load when the backend itself is hot

steps.title: Fair by construction
body:
• Shared capacity needs per-client budgets, or one bug becomes everyone's outage.
  • Fixed windows are simple but burst at edges; sliding windows smooth them.
  • Token buckets cap the average rate and allow controlled bursts.
  • With many gateways, keep counters in a shared store — and choose fail-open or fail-closed.
  • Reject cheaply with 429 + Retry-After so clients can back off.
